text:
Recency-based Sampling of Sequences (RSS) is not simply random prefix removal. It samples positive targets from throughout a history with probabilities favoring recent interactions, removes those targets, and encodes the remaining ordered interactions to predict the sampled set. Older interactions retain nonzero target probability, and early history largely remains available as context. RSS therefore changes the prediction objective rather than preserving strictly adjacent next-item supervision; it was evaluated with GRU4Rec as well as other architectures. [Petrov & Macdonald, RecSys 2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2207.02643)

Sequence cropping instead changes the available context. CL4SRec uses contiguous crops as contrastive views while retaining its original next-item recommendation loss; cropping need not discard the original supervised examples. By contrast, replacing training histories with suffixes removes older preference evidence from those examples. For matched next-item supervision, deleting a prefix from inputs x₁…xₜ requires retaining corresponding targets x₂…xₜ₊₁ at the surviving positions. An arbitrary interior crop paired with the original final target can introduce a prediction gap. [CL4SRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.14395), [EC4SRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.01347)

Implication for this experiment: stochastic suffix training may emphasize recent intent but weaken access to persistent preferences; training predominantly on short suffixes and evaluating longer histories also changes the GRU hidden-state distribution. These are plausible mechanisms, not established outcomes here. Compare unchanged GRU4Rec, deterministic recent-window truncation, and stochastic suffix cropping with matched targets, holding supervision and compute comparable. Include an uncropped-training probability to test the mismatch hypothesis. Cropping and recency bias have substantial precedent; novelty would require a more specific mechanism and evidence beyond random prefix removal.
